title: Your own commentary
hookLine: writing notes in the margin of your life
tomorrow: Eli asks a question Noa can't answer. does she have to answer it?

lines: A FURIOUS NO! IN THE MARGIN.
WHO WRITES IN A HOLY BOOK?
cards: A used paperback from a thrift store, and someone has written in it. An underline. A question mark.
A furious no! beside a plot twist. Sometimes the notes are the best part. So who writes in a holy book?
In Jewish tradition, readers do, starting with the very first verse. Rashi, the medieval commentator, stops at the Torah's opening words, In the beginning, and says something odd about them.
This verse, he writes, says only one thing: interpret me.

teach.h: WHY DOES THE FIRST VERSE NEED HELP?
teach.b: Why would the first verse need help? Rashi explains himself. If the verse meant to teach the order of creation, he says, it would have been worded differently.
The way it's written doesn't settle what came first. So he doesn't pretend it does. He leaves a note: this one is asking you to dig.
Here's the puzzle solved. The Torah, in this way of reading, isn't a finished statement you file away.
It's one side of a conversation, and the reader is expected to answer.

teach.h: THE TEXT IN THE MIDDLE, VOICES AROUND.
teach.b: That's why a printed page of the Talmud looks the way it does: the old text in the middle, and later voices in the margins around it, Rashi's notes running down the inside edge. Nobody erased the text to make room.
They wrote next to it. Your own commentary works the same way. A verse about seeking a city's peace, and in the margin, the name of your street.
A line about honoring parents, and beside it, a question you still can't answer about your own. You aren't changing the verse.
You're showing where it touched you.
Something to tell a friend tonight: one of Judaism's great commentators read the Torah's first sentence and wrote, in effect, this one needs a reader.

how: Jewish learners often read the Torah and Talmud alongside commentaries such as Rashi's, and some keep their own notes in the margins of a personal Chumash or study book.

o: a scholar's final ruling on what a verse means

games.q: the margin and the middle — tap the pairs.
p: the old text in the middle

s: writing your own comments on Torah is only for rabbis
the tradition reads with a pen; your own notes on a verse are part of how learning works.
Rashi says the Torah's first verse is asking to be interpreted
he says it doesn't settle the order of creation as written, so it says: interpret me.
a commentary replaces the verse it explains
on the page the text stays in the middle. the comments sit next to it.

games.q: you're reading a verse with your study partner and one word bugs you. it doesn't seem to fit. what would Rashi do?
o: write down what bugs you; the odd spot is where to dig.
skip it; the verse means what most people say it means.
look up the official meaning and cross out your question.
games.why: Rashi stops at the Torah's first words and says they ask to be interpreted. the strange spot is the invitation.

practice: Pick one verse or line you know, from these lessons or from memory, and write it by hand. Underneath, in small letters, write one comment: a question it raises, a person it reminds you of, or a place in your week where it fits.
Read the two together once, slowly.

wordCard.voice: Your own commentary: notes in the margin of a text, and of a life. The verse stays the same; your answer to it is yours.

orig.note: Hebrew: commentary, an explanation. Rashi's notes are called his perush on the Torah.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: your own margin, because even the first verse of the Torah asked for a reader. Talk soon.

sources.ref: Rashi on Genesis 1:1 (this verse says only: interpret me; it does not come to teach the order of creation)
